title: CWB Kitten Boatbuilding Project

# CWB KITTEN BOATBUILDING PROJECT

## Welcome, Lucile, to the CWB fleet!

The Center for Wooden Boats launched its first traditionally built sailing vessel in over 15 years: a Kitten Class gaff-rigged catboat designed by John Winslow in 1920 — and the first wooden boat built in the Wagner Education Center.

Three years earlier, Lead Boatwright Josh Anderson (now Executive Director) started a boatbuilding program and chose to rebuild a historic Lake Union design. A volunteer team had found an original Kitten hull on Vashon Island around 2008. The Kitten was one of the Seattle Yacht Club's first single-class youth sailing boats, built by Blanchard Boat Company in the 1920s. The project was chosen to accompany the "Still Afloat" exhibit as an interactive display.

The original plans were found in a 1920 magazine issue at the Seattle Public Library and scaled up for construction. Building began in September 2018 through 17 class modules; well over a hundred students, interns, volunteers, and staff took part over two years, using traditional methods and materials — Larch planking, White Oak frames, and Sitka Spruce spars. Each class module was independent, with no prerequisites.

*Contructing the Kitten.*

Naming rights were auctioned at CWB's March 2019 fundraiser. David James named the boat *Lucile*, after his late wife, at a christening ceremony on October 16, 2020.

*The christening ceremony for Lucile!*

## Kitten History

John Winslow designed the Kitten in 1920 to teach young sailors (originally young women) to sail. After moving to Seattle in 1922, he modified the design with Ted Geary and Norm Blanchard, making it the first self-rescuing dinghy on Puget Sound. No seaworthy wooden Kittens are known to exist today.

## About The Kitten: Lucile

- Length overall: 15 ft
- Beam: 6 ft
- Sail area: 163 sq ft
- Maximum draft: 8 in

**Credits:** Lead instructor Ben Kahn; sailmaker and rigger Sean Rankin (NW Sails and Canvas); caulker Brad Seamans (Port Townsend Shipwrights Co-Op); hardware from Port Townsend Foundry and Ed Louchard (Zephyrwerks); paint from Kirby Paint Co.

This project was supported in part by 4Culture/King County Lodging Tax.
